Lessons.Title: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Vertex Form
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use completing the square to convert standard and factored quadratic expressions into vertex form, revealing vertex and minimum/maximum while preserving the exact same function. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 22 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/22/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/22/index.html (CC BY 4.0). Source revisits why each form shows different graph features.

Original f(x)=x²−6x+5. To complete, add and subtract9: f=(x²−6x+9)−9+5=(x−3)²−4. Vertex(3,−4), opening upward and minimum−4. In factored form f=(x−1)(x−5), so roots1,5. Standard form gives y-intercept5. All three descriptions represent one function.

Second scaled example g(x)=2x²+8x+3=2(x²+4x)+3=2[(x+2)²−4]+3=2(x+2)²−5, giving vertex(−2,−5). It is essential to factor leading coefficient2 before completing the inner square; otherwise vertical shift may be wrong.

Student task: rewrite two quadratics from standard form, match each representation to what it reveals most efficiently (zeros, vertical intercept, vertex), and verify one symmetric pair. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for complete-square algebra, equivalence check, graph feature interpretation and form-selection explanation.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Balance added value inside same expression.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Completing nonmonic expression without extracting leading factor

SummaryPoints: Completing square rewrites, not changes, a quadratic function.
Vertex form makes extrema immediately visible.
Both monic and nonmonic conversion need correct balancing constants.
